beats.headline: Is your database managed by Hibernate?
beats.subline: If you use ddl-auto=update in production, you are one deployment away from a total outage.
beats.narration: If your production database schema is managed by Hibernate ddl-auto update, you are one deployment away from a total outage. It cannot safely rename columns or handle complex constraints. You need versioned migrations.

beats.title: The Migration Lifecycle
beats.subtitle: Versioned scripts ensure environment parity
beats.narration: Flyway and Liquibase treat schema changes like code. You define versioned scripts that run in order. The runner tracks state in a metadata table, ensuring every environment—from local to production—is identical.

beats.title: Flyway Naming Rules

steps.explanation: Versioned migrations run once. The double underscore is mandatory—forget it, and Flyway ignores your file.
Repeatable migrations run whenever the checksum changes. Perfect for views and stored procedures.

beats.narration: Flyway relies on strict naming. Use V for versioned scripts that run once, and R for repeatable scripts like views. That double underscore is non-negotiable; miss it, and your migration simply won't run.

beats.title: Flyway vs Liquibase
beats.narration: Flyway is the gold standard for SQL-heavy teams. Liquibase offers more abstraction with YAML or XML, which helps if you need to support multiple database engines like Oracle and Postgres simultaneously.

beats.title: Migrations Locked
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 2): How to avoid production table locks →
beats.narration: That's the foundation. In Part 2, we tackle the silent killer: how a simple ALTER TABLE can lock your entire production database.

beats.headline: Why did your migration take down production?
beats.subline: PostgreSQL locks are FIFO. A single slow query can queue your DDL and starve your app.
beats.narration: Why did a simple metadata change take down your production site? In Postgres, DDL locks are FIFO. If your migration queues behind a long-running report, every new request piles up behind it, exhausting your connection pool.

beats.title: The Lock Timeout Fix
beats.caption: Fail fast instead of queuing

lines.text: -- Always set a lock timeout for DDL
ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN status text;
ERROR: canceling statement due to lock timeout

beats.narration: Always set a lock timeout. If your migration can't grab the lock in two seconds, it should fail immediately. This prevents a cascade of blocked connections and gives your pipeline a chance to retry.

beats.title: Concurrent Indexing
beats.code:
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_users_email 
    ON users (email);

-- V12.sql.conf
executeInTransaction=false

steps.explanation: Avoids blocking writes during the index build. Essential for large production tables.
Postgres forbids concurrent index creation inside a transaction block. Disable it in your config file.

beats.narration: Standard index creation blocks writes. Use CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY instead. Just remember: Postgres forbids this inside a transaction block, so you must explicitly disable transactions for that specific migration file.

beats.title: Constraint Validation
beats.subtitle: Split heavy scans into two steps
beats.narration: Adding a NOT NULL constraint on a huge table will lock it. Instead, add it as NOT VALID to enforce it for new rows, then run VALIDATE in a separate step to scan existing data without blocking.

beats.title: Locking Strategies Locked
beats.narration: You're now safe from production locks. In Part 3, we master the Expand-and-Contract pattern to ship breaking schema changes with zero downtime.

beats.headline: How do you rename a column without downtime?
beats.subline: In a rolling deployment, old and new code run simultaneously. One wrong ALTER TABLE breaks everything.
beats.narration: How do you rename a column during a rolling deployment? You can't just drop the old one. Old pods will crash instantly. You need the Expand-and-Contract pattern to keep both versions happy.

beats.title: Expand-and-Contract
beats.subtitle: Safe, multi-release schema evolution
beats.narration: First, add the new column and dual-write from your app. Second, backfill existing rows in small, throttled batches. Finally, once all old pods are gone, you can safely drop the legacy column.

beats.title: Throttled Data Backfill
beats.code:
UPDATE users 
SET display_name = full_name 
WHERE id IN (
    SELECT id FROM users 
    WHERE display_name IS NULL 
    LIMIT 5000
);

steps.explanation: Never update millions of rows at once. Use LIMIT to keep transactions short and WAL growth manageable.

beats.narration: Never update millions of rows in one go. You'll bloat your transaction logs and kill performance. Use a loop with a LIMIT to process data in small, safe chunks.

beats.title: Transactional DDL
beats.narration: Postgres supports transactional DDL, so failed migrations roll back automatically. MySQL triggers an implicit commit after every statement, which makes partial failures a nightmare to clean up.

beats.title: Zero-Downtime Locked
beats.narration: You are now a migration expert. In Part 4, we wrap up with the final checklist and the lab link to test these skills.

beats.headline: Ready to ship schema changes safely?
beats.subline: Avoid drift, prevent locks, and embrace the expand-and-contract pattern.
beats.narration: Ready to ship schema changes without fear? Avoid drift, prevent locks, and embrace the expand-and-contract pattern. Your database is the most important part of your application; treat it with the respect it deserves.

beats.title: Migration Best Practices
beats.subtitle: The senior engineer's checklist
beats.narration: Treat migrations as code reviews. Keep DDL fast with lock timeouts, and always move heavy data operations out of the migration script and into asynchronous background jobs.

beats.title: When Checksums Fail
beats.caption: Don't panic—repair correctly

lines.text: # 2. Revert the file, add a new V-script

beats.narration: If you see a checksum mismatch, never edit the old file. Revert the changes to the original state, then add a new forward migration. Use flyway repair only to clean up failed rows.

beats.title: Versioning Strategy
beats.narration: For teams, use timestamps instead of sequential numbers. It eliminates merge conflicts entirely, ensuring your migrations never collide when multiple developers are working on the same branch.
